messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

During his assignment covering a remote border conflict, Dara was taken by a militia unit that suspected him of being a spy. For three days they held him in a concrete cell, and on the second day they began what they called "questioning." He remembers the smell of diesel and sweat, the way the light from a single bulb threw distorted shadows. But what he cannot shake—what he has never been able to fully retrieve in a coherent sequence—is the precise moment when the first blow landed. When he tries to deliberately recall what happened, the memory fragments into a series of disconnected images: a boot, the taste of blood, a man’s voice saying something in a language he almost understood. It feels so extreme that part of him still struggles to believe it actually happened to him. There are gaps he cannot fill no matter how hard he tries.

In the months after his release and return to the United States, Dara tried to resume his work as a journalist, but the world had become a different place. He found himself jumping at ordinary sounds—the clatter of a dropped pen in the newsroom, the sudden ring of a telephone—and these startle responses left him flushed and ashamed. He began watching his colleagues closely, scanning their faces for any flicker of hostility, certain that someone might be planning to harm him. What frightened him most, though, was the conviction that others could see what had been done to him just by looking at him. He became convinced there was something fundamentally wrong with him as a person, that he had acted in ways during the captivity that violated who he believed himself to be—he had begged, he had wept, he had given them the names of sources. He dwelled endlessly on how the event could have been prevented, replaying decisions he had made at the border crossing, each revision more punishing than the last.

One afternoon in the grocery store, a child began to cry two aisles over. Dara’s chest tightened instantly; the sound seemed to pierce through him, and he felt dizzy, the fluorescent lights swimming. In that moment, the fragmented memory surged back—not as a clear narrative, but as a visceral wave of heat and dread. He abandoned his cart and walked out, certain that the crying child had somehow known, that everyone in the store was staring at the marks they could surely see on him. The next time he heard a child cry in a parking lot, he stopped going to that shopping center entirely. He also began avoiding seeing people he had socialized with before the event; their casual questions about his assignment felt like interrogation, and their sympathetic looks confirmed that they could read the shame written across his face. Hearing names that reminded him of his captors—common names, ordinary names—sent him retreating into himself, and he found himself restricting food as a way of regaining some small measure of control over a body that no longer felt like his own. The more he avoided eating, the more his mind seemed to drift back into the gaps of the memory, as though starvation might finally unlock what he could not consciously reach.

His threat monitoring only intensified the cycle. Each time he started at a sound, he felt more defective; each time he watched others for signs of danger, he became more convinced that they could see his violation. The dizziness that sometimes overtook him in crowded spaces would trigger a flash of the cell, and then the negative appraisals would surge again—he was broken, he was exposed, he had betrayed himself. He began to interpret every ordinary sound as a potential threat, and every potential threat as confirmation that the world remained unsafe and that he remained its target. His avoidance of social contacts meant he spent long evenings alone in his apartment, and in that solitude the memory would press in harder, the gaps feeling more like accusations than absences. The undereating left him lightheaded, and that somatic dizziness became another trigger, a loop that tightened week by week.

What finally brought Dara to seek help was a moment in the newsroom when a colleague called his name—a name that shared its first syllable with one of his captors—and he found himself on the floor, his heart hammering, unable to speak. He had stopped going to work after that. Now he sits in a therapist’s office, afraid that talking about what happened will make the gaps close into something worse, but even more afraid of living the rest of his life in a world where a child’s cry can undo him.
